text: Albert-László Barabási, born March 30, 1967, in Cârța, Harghita County, Romania, to an ethnic Hungarian family, is a Romanian-born Hungarian-American physicist renowned for his pioneering work in network science and network medicine. His father, László Barabási, was a historian, museum director, and writer, while his mother, Katalin Keresztes, taught literature and later directed a children's theater. Barabási attended a high school specializing in science and mathematics, where he won a local physics olympiad in both the 9th and 12th grades. Between 1986 and 1989, he studied physics and engineering at the University of Bucharest, during which he began researching chaos theory and published three papers. In 1989, he emigrated to Hungary with his father and earned a master's degree in 1991 at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest under Tamás Vicsek. He then pursued a PhD in physics at Boston University, completing it in 1994 under H. Eugene Stanley, with his thesis titled *Fractal Concepts in Surface Growth* published by Cambridge University Press. After a one-year postdoc at the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, Barabási joined the University of Notre Dame in 1995, becoming the Emil T. Hofmann Professor of Physics in 2000 at age 32, making him the youngest endowed professor. In 2004, he founded the Center for Complex Network Research. He served as a visiting professor at Harvard University in 2005–06 and, in fall 2007, moved to Northeastern University as a Distinguished University Professor and director of the Center for Network Science, while also holding an appointment in the Department of Medicine at Harvard Medical School. He is the founding president of the Network Science Society and sponsors the NetSci Conference, established in 2006. As of 2008, Barabási holds Hungarian, Romanian, and U.S. citizenship. In 1999, he discovered scale-free networks and proposed the Barabási–Albert model, which explains how growth and preferential attachment lead to the emergence of such networks in natural, technological, and social systems, including the World Wide Web and online communities. He created a map of the World Wide Web and found its degree distribution follows a power law, not a Poisson distribution, and later demonstrated that power-law distributions also appear in metabolic and protein–protein interaction networks, showing the universality of scale-free properties. In 2001, with Réka Albert and Hawoong Jeong, he showed that networks are robust to random failures but vulnerable to targeted attacks—a phenomenon known as the Achilles' heel property—linking the breakdown threshold to the second moment of the degree distribution. In 2016, he extended these ideas to network resilience, defining it as a dynamical property involving adaptation to disturbances without losing functionality. Barabási is recognized as one of the founders of network medicine, a concept introduced in his 2007 article "Network Medicine – From Obesity to the 'Diseasome'" in *The New England Journal of Medicine*, where he introduced the concept of the diseasome, illustrating how diseases are interconnected through shared genetic factors. He pioneered the use of large patient datasets to link disease comorbidity to molecular networks and established that genes associated with the same disease reside in the same network neighborhood, leading to the concept of disease modules used in drug discovery and biomarker development. His work led to the establishment of the Channing Division of Network Medicine at Harvard Medical School and the Network Medicine Institute, which includes 33 universities and institutions worldwide. His research has generated experimentally falsifiable predictions, including identifying novel pathways in asthma, predicting the mechanism of action for rosmarinic acid, and enabling drug repurposing. In clinical settings, his work helps physicians determine whether rheumatoid arthritis patients will respond to anti-TNF therapy. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he led a collaboration with researchers from Harvard University, Boston University, and The Broad Institute to predict and test the efficacy of 6,000 approved drugs for COVID patients. In 2005, he discovered that human activity patterns exhibit fat-tailed interevent times, indicating bursty behavior—short bursts of activity followed by long inactive periods—leading to the development of the Barabási model of human dynamics, detailed in his book *Bursts: The Hidden Pattern Behind Everything We Do*. In 2008, using anonymized mobile phone data, he published in *Nature* that human movement is highly regular, with consistent travel distances and frequent returns to visited locations, and in a 2010 *Science* paper found a 93% predictability of human movement across all users, introducing two principles governing human trajectories that led to a widely used mobility model. A decade before the COVID-19 pandemic, he used this model to predict virus spreading patterns through direct contact. Barabási made foundational contributions to network controllability and observability by applying control theory tools to network science, proposing a method to identify control nodes by mapping the control problem into graph matching, merging statistical mechanics and control theory. He applied these principles to predict the functions of neurons in the *Caenorhabditis elegans* connectome, successfully identifying new neurons involved in locomotion and confirming the validity of the predictions. He received the 2024 Gothenburg Lise Meitner Award, the 2023 Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize from the American Physical Society for pioneering work on the statistical physics of networks and for communicating the significance of the field, the 2021 EPS Statistical and Nonlinear Physics Prize for his contributions to complex network science, including scale-free networks, preferential attachment, network robustness, controllability, social ties, communities, human mobility, and biological networks, and the 2021 ranking as the world’s second-best engineering and technology scientist based on h-index. He has been elected to the US National Academy of Sciences, the Austrian Academy of Sciences (2024), the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (2004), Academia Europaea (2007), the European Academy of Sciences and Art (2018), the Romanian Academy of Sciences (2018), and the Massachusetts Academy of Sciences (2013), and is a Fellow of the American Physical Society (2003), the American Association for the Advancement of Science (2011), and the Network Science Society (2021). He has also received a Doctor Honoris Causa from Obuda University (2023), the Technical University of Madrid (2011), Utrecht University (2018), and West University of Timișoara (2020), the Bolyai Prize from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (2019), the Senior Scientific Award of the Complex Systems Society (2017) for setting the foundation of modern network science, the Lagrange Prize (2011), the C&C Prize (2008) from Japan for discovering the scale-free property in real-world networks, the Cozzarelli Prize from the National Academies of Sciences (USA), the John von Neumann Medal (2006) from the John von Neumann Computer Society, and the FEBS Anniversary Prize for Systems Biology (2005). In 2019, with Giulia Menichetti, he identified that conventional nutritional databases track only a small fraction of the over 26,000 biochemicals in food, coining the term "nutritional dark matter," which inspired the Periodic Table of Food Initiative by the Rockefeller Foundation and the American Heart Association. In 2021, he extended network medicine to study polyphenols, showing how molecular networks link dietary compounds to health outcomes. He developed the first AI tool to predict food processing levels, showing that over 73% of the U.S. food supply is ultra-processed and correlating processing with adverse health markers. His efforts culminated in the 2025 release of GroceryDB and the TrueFood database, used daily by millions to reveal food processing levels in U.S. supermarkets.
